summarize

/SUM-uh-rize/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Summarize means to restate something in a much shorter form, keeping only the main points and letting the details fall away.

Asked about the four-hour hearing, the aide summarized it in a single line: the vote will be close, and it will be Tuesday.

Example

The new ranger noticed that nobody read the forty pages of trail regulations posted in the trailhead kiosk. Over the winter she summarized them onto a single carved sign — stay on the marked path, pack out what you pack in, camp only below the tree line — and rule-breaking fell by half before summer.

Forty pages became three essentials. Cutting a long text down to the few points that matter most, and letting everything else go, is exactly what it means to summarize.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

condense: Condense means to press something into less space while keeping all of its essential content — a condensed book keeps every chapter, just tighter. Summarize goes further: you keep only the main points and deliberately let the details fall away.

recap: Recap means to run back quickly over what has already been said or happened, usually right afterward and for someone catching up — a coach recaps the first half at halftime. Summarize is the broader act of reducing any material to its main points, spoken or written, at any distance from the original.

paraphrase: Paraphrase means to restate someone's words in your own words at about the same length and level of detail — it changes the wording, not the amount. Summarize changes the amount: a summary is drastically shorter than what it restates.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

elaborate: to develop at greater length, adding detail rather than cutting it

transcribe: to copy out in full, word for word, with nothing dropped

Where it sits · how far the material is boiled down

recap → summarize → distill

recap vs. summarize: Recap is lighter than summarize: a recap quickly runs back over what just happened for someone catching up, while to summarize is the fuller work of pulling every main point out of the whole.

distill vs. summarize: Distill goes further than summarize: summarizing keeps all of the main points, while distilling boils the material down to its single purest idea and lets even minor points go.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — summ-: the total; the highest point (Latin summa)

Suffix — -ar-: of, connected with (the ending that forms 'summary')

Suffix — -ize: to make; to perform the act of

Put it together: Latin summa meant 'the total' — and because Roman accountants added their columns from the bottom up, the finished total sat at the top of the page, which is why summus also meant 'highest.' To summarize is literally to deliver the summa: the total of a text, given at the top level, with the small figures left below.

Use the root in a new word: summation: The jury leaned forward as the young defense attorney rose to begin her summation.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral — the everyday workhorse

Summarize is the plain, everyday verb for shrinking material to its main points, equally at home in a classroom and a boardroom. Keep it apart from paraphrase, which changes the wording but not the amount, and from condense, which squeezes everything tighter without discarding anything. If you kept only what matters most, you summarized. The thing you produce is a summary.
